# [T]{.k-t} — Transferable {#transferable}

::: {.tada-key}
**Transferability** is the ability for anyone to open the file, view and run
the code **without conversion or alteration**. It covers the FAIR principle of
interoperability — anyone can open and use your code — and extends it so that
the code also runs on **different computers and operating systems**.
:::

Two things make code transferable, and they are independent. Get one wrong and
the other does not save you.

1. The code is saved in a **file type any text editor or IDE can open**.
2. The code contains **no paths specific to your machine**.

## Save code in an interoperable file type {#transferable-filetype}

Save code with an extension that matches the language: **`.R`**, **`.py`**,
**`.cpp`**, or the equivalent standard format. These can be viewed, edited and
saved by any text editor or IDE (RStudio, VS Code, PyCharm) on any system.

**Do not share code inside `.PDF` or `.docx` files.** A PDF can be *viewed*,
but it cannot be opened and edited in an IDE without extra libraries or
software, or without converting it to another file type first.

::: {.tada-warn}
The deeper problem with PDFs and Word documents is what happens when someone
copies out of them. Copy-pasting from these formats can change characters —
apostrophes are the classic — alter white space, or drag in unwanted extras
such as line numbers and headers. The result is code errors that are
**sometimes difficult to spot or time consuming to fix**, because the code
looks correct.
:::

**A note on `.txt`.** A plain text file does let people copy and paste without
those problems. But it causes a different issue: many IDEs interpret the coding
language from the extension. Without the `.R` extension, an IDE may not
recognise the file as R and may not let you execute it until you re-save it as
`.R`. Use the language's own extension.

**If your language does not use a standard file type**, apply this test: *can
the resulting file be opened by a text editor?* SPSS syntax `.sps` files, for
example, can be read in a text editor, so they pass.

## Avoid local and user-specific file paths {#transferable-paths}

This is the single most common cause of code that "worked when I sent it".

File paths must be written so they do not depend on your local environment or
directory structure. That means **relative** file paths rather than local or
user-specific ones. It also means putting **data, code, and all necessary
materials in a single project directory** — relative paths have to be relative
to *something*.

::: {.tada-compare}
::: {.tada-before}
Before

```r
setwd("C:/Users/ed/Desktop/caterpillar_paper/analysis")
dat <- read.csv("caterpillars_2024.csv")
```

Sets a working directory that exists on exactly one computer, running one
operating system, belonging to one person. Everyone else gets an error before
the data is even loaded.
:::

::: {.tada-after}
After

```r
library(here)
dat <- read.csv(here("data", "raw", "caterpillars_2024.csv"))
```

Agnostic of operating system and of where the project folder sits. Anyone who
downloads the project can load the data.
:::
:::

### How to do it {.unlisted .unnumbered}

There are several options, and they combine.

::: {.tabset}

#### R {.unlisted .unnumbered}

**Use an RStudio project.** *File → New Project* creates a `.Rproj` file. Open
the project and RStudio automatically sets the working directory to the project
folder, so you never need `setwd()` at all.
See <https://docs.posit.co/ide/user/ide/get-started/>.

**Use the `here` package** (Müller & Bryan 2020). `here()` builds paths
relative to the project directory, whatever the operating system:

```r
library(here)

raw     <- read.csv(here("data", "raw", "caterpillars_2024.csv"))
clean   <- here("data", "processed", "caterpillars_clean.csv")
figure  <- here("output", "figures", "fig3_abundance.png")
```

**Use both.** The TADA authors recommend RStudio projects *and* `here` together
to maximise transferability across operating systems.

**Without an IDE**, launching R from inside the project directory achieves a
similar effect.

::: {.tada-warn}
Whatever you do, avoid `setwd()`. It sets a path that is specific to both the
operating system and the user, and it is the thing that causes other people to
hit errors when they run your code.
:::

#### Python {.unlisted .unnumbered}

**Use `pyprojroot`** (Chen 2023), which creates file paths relative to the
project directory regardless of operating system — the Python counterpart to
`here`:

```python
from pyprojroot import here
import pandas as pd

raw = pd.read_csv(here("data/raw/caterpillars_2024.csv"))
```

**Work inside the project directory.** Running an instance of Python within the
specific project folder removes the need for local file paths.

::: {.tada-warn}
Avoid `os.chdir()`, the Python equivalent of `setwd()`. It has the same
problem: it hard-codes a path that only exists on your machine.
:::

#### Other IDEs {.unlisted .unnumbered}

**VS Code.** Navigate to the project folder and open *the folder* (not the
individual file). This performs a similar action to using an RStudio project —
the workspace root becomes the reference point for relative paths.

**Standalone interpreters.** Launching R or Python from within the project
directory does the same thing: the working directory is the project, and every
path in the code can be relative to it.

**Any language.** The principle does not depend on the tool. Organise
everything into one project directory, then write every path relative to the
top of that directory.

:::

::: {.tada-note}
Whichever method you choose, **state it in the code documentation**. Someone
opening your project needs to know that they are expected to open the `.Rproj`
file, or activate a virtual environment, before running anything. See
[Documented](#documented).
:::

## Beyond TADA: environments and pipelines {#transferable-beyond}

Explicitly beyond the scope of TADA, but worth knowing, because both address
failures that relative paths alone cannot fix.

**Containerisation** — **Docker** (Merkel 2014) and **Singularity** (Kurtzer et
al. 2017) — uses images that encapsulate a complete software environment,
including all required programs and libraries. This helps ensure environment
reproducibility between systems and avoids the common *"works on my computer"*
problem.

**Workflow managers** — **Snakemake** (Köster & Rahmann 2012) and **Nextflow**
(Di Tommaso et al. 2017) — specify the sequence of scripts or computational
steps in a pipeline and their dependencies, ensuring each step executes in a
defined and reproducible order.

Neither is required by TADA. If you are already comfortable with them, they
strengthen transferability considerably. If not, relative paths and a good
README get you most of the way.

## Checklist {#transferable-checklist}

- [ ] Every script has a standard extension for its language (`.R`, `.py`, `.cpp`, …)
- [ ] No code is distributed only inside a `.pdf` or `.docx`
- [ ] Data, code and materials are all inside a single project directory
- [ ] No `setwd()` (R) or `os.chdir()` (Python) anywhere in the code
- [ ] No absolute paths (`/Users/…`, `C:/…`, `~/Dropbox/…`)
- [ ] Paths are built with `here()` / `pyprojroot`, or are relative to the project root
- [ ] The project opens via `.Rproj` / a virtual environment, and this is stated in the README
- [ ] Test: copy the project to a different folder (ideally a different machine) and run it
